edition.title: Morning Edition
edition.dek: A $25 billion privacy ruling; Ebola's cross-border spread; tentative Ukraine diplomacy; and a village of scarecrows.

lead_story.headline: New Mexico judge orders Meta to pay $25 billion over Facebook privacy claims
lead_story.summary: A state judge imposed a $25 billion civil penalty after a jury found Meta liable for misleading Facebook users about control over their personal information. Meta disputes the ruling and says it will appeal.
lead_story.why_it_matters: The unprecedented state-level penalty tests how consumer-protection law can hold major platforms accountable; collection and the final amount remain uncertain pending appeal.

items.headline: Ebola outbreak spreads across borders from Congo
items.summary: The World Health Organization says the fast-growing outbreak originating in eastern Congo has reached other countries, with Nigeria reporting a case and authorities tracing contacts. Case counts and transmission chains are still changing.
items.why_it_matters: Containment depends on rapid detection, protective equipment, cross-border coordination and public trust rather than borders alone.

items.headline: Russia agrees to restart three-way talks on Ukraine, Kremlin says
items.summary: Following a meeting with a U.S. envoy, the Kremlin said Vladimir Putin agreed to resume talks involving Moscow, Kyiv and Washington. A declared willingness to negotiate does not itself establish a ceasefire or agreement.
items.why_it_matters: Diplomatic movement matters only if it produces verifiable changes in fighting and negotiating positions.

items.headline: South Korean officials struggle to guide a shark back to open water
items.summary: Busan's rescue workers temporarily moved a large dusky shark out of a canal, but it swam back in. Fisheries experts say the animal's behavior and safe relocation remain uncertain.
items.why_it_matters: The episode shows the difficulty of managing wildlife in heavily engineered ports without harming an endangered animal.

items.headline: UN report warns current climate pledges leave world on hotter path
items.summary: The latest UN emissions assessment finds national commitments remain insufficient to meet international temperature goals, even if implemented as promised.
items.why_it_matters: Policy commitments and real-world emissions remain separate measures of progress.

items.headline: Older catch-up: Pompeii's grandest house begins privately funded restoration
items.summary: The House of Marcus Fabius Rufus, closed since 1980, is receiving a €1.4 million restoration funded by a German entrepreneur. Officials hope to reopen part of the complex to guided groups by Christmas.
items.why_it_matters: The project raises questions about conservation financing, public access and how archaeology is presented.

items.headline: Waterdown's scarecrow walk becomes an October neighborhood ritual
items.summary: More than 140 scarecrows made by businesses and volunteers line Waterdown Village in Ontario for the annual autumn walk, which includes a scavenger hunt and a planned pet-and-treat event.
items.why_it_matters: A modest community tradition shows how a shared street can become a seasonal project.

items.headline: Moral luck challenges our ideas of blame and desert
items.summary: Robert J. Hartman explores whether two people who take the same reckless risk deserve different moral judgments when chance means only one causes serious harm.
items.why_it_matters: The distinction between culpable choices and actual outcomes matters for criminal justice, forgiveness and how we judge others.

worth_your_time.headline: A former hostage examines whether he can forgive his captors
worth_your_time.summary: Michael Scott Moore recounts his captivity in Somalia and considers the relationship between personal forgiveness, responsibility and the criminal justice system.
worth_your_time.why_it_matters: The essay resists easy reconciliation and distinguishes understanding a perpetrator from excusing what happened.

https://aeon.co/essays/how-to-tell-a-bad.question: Should a person's blameworthiness change when luck changes the consequences of the same choice?
https://aeon.co/essays/how-to-tell-a-bad.thesis: The distinction between an agent's character, their reckless action and the resulting harm helps explain conflicting moral intuitions.
https://aeon.co/essays/how-to-tell-a-bad.argument: Two drivers may take the same unreasonable risk while only one harms someone. Equal recklessness supports an equal assessment of their choices; different harms can still generate different obligations to victims.
https://aeon.co/essays/how-to-tell-a-bad.intellectual_background: Moral luck is associated with Bernard Williams and Thomas Nagel, whose debates question whether moral judgment can escape circumstances beyond our control.
https://aeon.co/essays/how-to-tell-a-bad.example: Two people drive equally recklessly; one reaches home without incident while the other injures a pedestrian.
https://aeon.co/essays/how-to-tell-a-bad.strongest_objection: If blame tracks luck, moral desert seems arbitrary; if it ignores harm, victims' experiences disappear.
https://aeon.co/essays/how-to-tell-a-bad.possible_response: Separate judgments of character from responsibility for actual consequences and duties of repair.
https://aeon.co/essays/how-to-tell-a-bad.implications: Law, restitution and personal blame need not use identical standards.
unresolved_questions: Should punishment depend on harm or risk?
How much of character itself is luck?
